issues.legal_issue: A purchaser manufacturing bidis must obtain transport permits for moving purchased leaves from the purchasing unit to a warehouse, from the warehouse to branches, and from branches to contractors, but not for the contractors’ distribution of leaves to workers who roll the bidis.
material_facts: The purchasers bought leaves for manufacturing bidis and moved them from the units where they were purchased to warehouses, branches, and independent contractors.
The contractors distributed the leaves to a very large number of workers who rolled bidis.
The governing rules provided for transport permits, and the authorities required permits for movement to the contractors and for distribution to the workers.
issues.conclusion: The permit requirement applies to movement through delivery to the contractors, but not to the contractors’ distribution of leaves to the workers.
issues.legal_principle: The statutory language and rules must be read in light of the Act’s purpose and with a presumption in favour of constitutionality. Although the permit system covers movement from the purchasing unit to storage and onward to branches and contractors, the legislature did not intend to require permits for distribution to the numerous workers. This construction accords with Article 19(5) and (6) and Article 304(b) of the Constitution.

rule.if: transport_permit_dispute and leaves_purchased_for_bidi_manufacture and (leaves_moved_to_warehouse or leaves_moved_to_branch or leaves_moved_to_contractor) and contractors_distribute_leaves_to_many_workers

predicates.transport_permit_dispute: The proceeding challenges whether permits are required for transporting purchased leaves.
predicates.leaves_purchased_for_bidi_manufacture: A purchaser acquired leaves for use in manufacturing bidis.
predicates.leaves_moved_to_warehouse: The purchaser moved leaves from the purchasing area to a warehouse.
predicates.leaves_moved_to_branch: The purchaser moved leaves from a warehouse to a branch.
predicates.leaves_moved_to_contractor: The purchaser moved leaves from a branch to an independent contractor.
predicates.contractors_distribute_leaves_to_many_wo: Independent contractors distribute leaves to many workers who roll bidis.

issues.definition: When a permit dispute concerns leaves purchased for bidi manufacture and their movement through warehouses, branches, and contractors to numerous workers, permits are required through delivery to the contractors but not for the contractors’ distribution to the workers.

issues.legal_issue: Restrictions on transporting purchased leaves are ancillary to, rather than an integral part of, a State monopoly in their purchase and sale, and must be reasonable; the permit system is valid through delivery to contractors but is unreasonable insofar as it requires permits for distribution to workers.
material_facts: The statutory scheme created a State monopoly in purchasing and selling leaves, with prices fixed after consultation and the State required to purchase the stock offered by growers.
The purchasers moved leaves through warehouses, branches, and independent contractors before the leaves reached workers who rolled bidis.
The contractors and workers were numerous, so requiring permits for each distribution to workers would cause extraordinary inconvenience.
Manufacturers were required to keep stock accounts and submit returns, and authorities could inspect their records and stock.
issues.conclusion: Transport controls are not protected as an essential part of the monopoly and must satisfy the constitutional reasonableness test. The controls are valid for movement up to the contractors, but a permit requirement for distribution from contractors to workers is unreasonable. The relevant restrictions must be assessed under Article 19(5) and the first part of Article 19(6), as well as Article 304(b).
issues.legal_principle: Under Akadasi Padhan v. State of Orissa, only provisions basically and essentially necessary to create a State monopoly are protected by the latter part of Article 19(6); subsidiary or incidental provisions must independently satisfy the applicable reasonableness test. Restrictions on transport after purchase are ancillary to the monopoly in purchase and sale. The burden of bringing an infringing restriction within the constitutional protections rests on those supporting it, as stated in Saghir Ahmad v. State of U.P. and Khyerbari Tea Co. Ltd. v. State of Assam. Article 304(b) applies the same reasonableness yardstick here.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_transport_controls and state_monopoly_covers_purchase_and_sale and transport_occurs_after_purchase and movement_checks_help_prevent_illicit_transactions and permits_at_each_worker_distribution_cause_extraordinary_inconvenience and manufacturer_records_and_inspection_provide_checks

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_transport_co: A proceeding challenges the constitutionality of restrictions on transporting goods after purchase.
predicates.state_monopoly_covers_purchase_and_sale: The State has reserved the purchase and sale of the commodity to itself and its authorised representatives.
predicates.transport_occurs_after_purchase: The disputed movement occurs after the goods have been purchased and ownership has passed to the purchaser.
predicates.movement_checks_help_prevent_illicit_tra: The State relies on movement controls to help detect illicit acquisitions or transactions.
predicates.permits_at_each_worker_distribution_caus: Requiring permits for each distribution to numerous workers would cause extraordinary inconvenience to the manufacturing process.
predicates.manufacturer_records_and_inspection_prov: Manufacturers keep stock records and returns, and public authorities can inspect them.

issues.definition: When transport controls follow a State monopoly in purchase and sale, help prevent illicit transactions, and are supported by manufacturer records and inspection, they may remain valid through delivery to contractors, but not if permitting each distribution to numerous workers causes extraordinary inconvenience.

issues.legal_issue: A restriction on movement of leaves already in stock when the transport rules took effect is not invalid merely because it also applies to that existing stock.
material_facts: An administrative order prohibited movement of old leaves, which in this context meant leaves in stock when the rules took effect.
The Court considered that order along with the transport restrictions and upheld the restrictions except for requiring a permit for distribution to workers.
issues.conclusion: The restriction on movement of old leaves, understood as leaves already in stock when the rules took effect, was not successfully challenged, subject to the exception for permits for distribution to workers.
issues.legal_principle: The transport restrictions must be construed and assessed for reasonableness in light of their purpose and practical effects. The Court upheld the restrictions on movement, including the order concerning old stock, except to the extent that a permit was required for distribution to workers; the applicable constitutional standards were Article 19(5) and (6) and Article 304(b).

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_existing_sto: A proceeding challenges a restriction on moving goods that were already held in stock.
predicates.restriction_covers_goods_already_in_stoc: The restriction applies to goods held in stock when the transport controls began.
predicates.restriction_operates_as_part_of_transpor: The restriction forms part of a system regulating movement of the goods.

issues.definition: When a challenged movement restriction covers goods already in stock as part of a transport-control system, the restriction remains valid except insofar as it requires permits for distribution to workers.

issues.legal_issue: Rescinding an administrative concession that allowed a regulated person to issue transport permits is not itself an unreasonable restriction on business.
material_facts: An officer temporarily allowed branch managers to issue permits for movement of leaves to contractors.
The officer rescinded that concession after finding that the managers were issuing permits for bulk transport contrary to the purpose of the concession.
issues.conclusion: The rescission of the concession could not be challenged as an unreasonable restriction.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the later order as the cancellation of a concession, rather than as an independent restriction on business, and held that its cancellation was not an unreasonable restriction.

predicates.challenge_to_rescission_of_administrativ: A proceeding challenges an official’s withdrawal of a previously granted administrative concession.
predicates.official_previously_allowed_private_issu: An official had allowed private persons to issue transport permits.
predicates.private_issuers_used_concession_for_bulk: The private persons used the permission to issue permits for bulk transport.

issues.definition: When a proceeding challenges withdrawal of permission for private persons to issue transport permits after they used it for bulk transport, the withdrawal is not an unreasonable restriction.
